blocks.text: Gu You Talks “The First Taste of Loneliness”, Shanshui Painting, Family, the Moon and Finding New Possibilities in Cinema
Gu You discusses family, loneliness, shanshui painting, moon symbolism and the formal rules behind “The First Taste of Loneliness”.

Gu You, the filmmaker previously known professionally as Gu Xiaogang, continues his exploration of the relationship between traditional Chinese art and contemporary cinema with “ The First Taste of Loneliness ”. Built around three women from different generations, the film approaches family without the constant conflict that frequently defines the genre, while using the moon, long takes and carefully controlled camera movement to connect intimate emotions with broader philosophical questions about loneliness, happiness and the meaning of life.
The First Taste of Loneliness is screening at Busan International Film Festival

Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Gu first explained the decision to adopt the name Gu You. His legal identity remains Gu Xiaogang; the change is closer to the traditional Chinese practice in which historical figures could be known by more than one name, or to the modern idea of an artistic name. The choice emerged from his increasingly deep engagement with shanshui painting , an ancient Chinese art form that has become central to his filmmaking and his thinking about cinema.

That interest is visible not only aesthetically but also in the emotional structure of “The First Taste of Loneliness”. While many contemporary Chinese family dramas focus on resentment, arguments and damage passed between relatives, Gu deliberately wanted something different. He acknowledges that conflict-heavy family narratives often resemble real life, particularly within a culture where people may struggle to express affection directly. But precisely because of that reality, he wanted his three female characters to care for one another openly, share their fears and eventually communicate their love.

For Gu, this choice was also personal. He wanted to make something that his own family—or other Chinese families—might watch and take some warmth from. Cinema, in that sense, could become a small encouragement toward expressing feelings that are often left unspoken. The absence of major domestic confrontation is therefore not an attempt to idealize family life, but a conscious decision to imagine another possibility for how people might relate to each other.

The names and identities of the three women are closely connected with the moon, one of the film’s central philosophical images. Gu explains that the film could almost have been called “The First Taste of Happiness” or even “The First Taste of the Meaning of Life”. Within the Chinese Zen tradition as he understands it, the full moon can represent an ultimate form of meaning or happiness: something complete, constant and always present even when human experience changes beneath it.

The three women consequently represent different stages and experiences of life, including love, family, relationships, separation and death. Gu compares their experiences to reflections of the same moon appearing on different bodies of water. The reflection may change depending on whether it falls on a river, lake or sea, but the moon itself remains whole. Pain, loneliness and happiness therefore become different experiences through which a person can move closer to understanding what actually matters.

This philosophical approach also shaped the film’s distinctive visual grammar. Before shooting began, Gu and his team established six rules governing how the movie could be filmed, somewhat in the spirit of filmmakers imposing formal restrictions on themselves. One of the most important was that camera movement should proceed from right to left, inspired by the directional movement found in ancient Chinese visual documents and paintings.

Another principle involved creating transitions between different spaces and even different moments of time within a single shot. Gu connects this to traditional Chinese painting, where one image can contain multiple spaces and temporal experiences rather than following a single fixed perspective. The long take therefore becomes more than a stylistic signature. It allows geography, time and emotion to shift inside the same composition.

The restrictions were also a response to contemporary technological freedom. In an era when digital tools and artificial intelligence make almost any visual effect possible, Gu became interested in the opposite approach: restricting what he could do in order to discover possibilities that might otherwise remain invisible. Rather than treating technological freedom as inherently creative, he believes clearly defined limitations can force filmmakers to reconsider the basic language of cinema.

The final scene demonstrates how visual form and the film’s emotional ideas come together. Gu clarified that a sound heard after the protagonist leaves is not something breaking, but the closing of a door. Her departure leaves the apartment empty, but the absence is important because there is another form of loneliness present throughout the film that audiences may not immediately recognize: that of the dead grandfather.

Gu explains that the camera can be understood as carrying the perspective of the grandfather’s soul. The film becomes, in part, the story of his final hundred days of saying goodbye to the three women. When Jiang Yue finally leaves and the door closes, the empty frame represents not only her departure but the loneliness of the person who has already died and remains connected to those who continue living. The long takes thus have an emotional function beyond their connection to shanshui aesthetics.

Preparing the actresses required an equally unusual process. Gu rented the apartment used in the film well before principal photography and asked the three women to live there together. There were no crew members, assistants or managers present—only the actresses and Gu himself observing. They cooked, slept, used the bathroom, learned where objects were kept and gradually became accustomed to sharing the space as though they were genuinely a family. Only after establishing that familiarity did shooting begin.

Casting itself was connected partly to geography and temperament. Gu was interested in performers who had some relationship to Zhejiang and who could feel naturally connected to the place. In choosing Zhou Xun, he also considered the public impression surrounding her: someone thoughtful and interested in larger questions about life. That quality matched Jiang Yue, whose father’s death sends her toward her own search for meaning. Gu felt Chinese audiences could therefore intuitively believe in her journey.

Despite the film’s apparently simple construction, editing became unexpectedly difficult. “The First Taste of Loneliness” consists of only around 50 shots, with more than 20 of them extended takes. Gu initially assumed such a limited amount of footage would make post-production comparatively straightforward. Instead, the editing process stretched across approximately a year, with periods of two or three months between different versions. Chinese director

The difficulty was philosophical rather than technical. Gu compares it to a Chinese saying suggesting that characters made with very few brushstrokes can be among the hardest to write correctly. With so few cuts available, every decision carried additional weight. More importantly, he was still asking himself throughout writing, production and editing what loneliness actually means. The movie could not be completed simply by finding the right technical rhythm; he first had to continue confronting the question at its center. Chinese director

His next work will continue investigating the relationship between shanshui painting and cinema , although Gu is now considering moving the experiment in another direction. While the rules of “The First Taste of Loneliness” primarily governed cinematography and visual language, the next project may apply a similar principle to genre itself. He is considering whether romance, the road movie, crime or another established form can be rethought through the principles he has been developing from traditional painting.

The goal, however, remains consistent. Gu is less interested in reproducing traditional Chinese art on screen than in asking what its ideas can offer contemporary cinema. “The First Taste of Loneliness” uses family, the moon, empty rooms and moving images to bring emotional experience into contact with something more philosophical. In doing so, Gu continues searching for a cinematic language in which ancient forms can generate genuinely new possibilities.
